shortDescription: In Antioch, in Roman Syria, bishops met many times over their bishop, Paul of Samosata, and put him out of the church for what he taught about Christ. Later Lucian, a presbyter of Antioch, died for his faith, and Arius called himself his pupil.

timeline.when: Before Paul, under Serapion and Asclepiades
timeline.headline: Serapion, bishop of Antioch, writes against the New Prophecy and on a gospel read at Rhossus

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Serapion, who by report succeeded Maximinus as bishop of Antioch, wrote against the New Prophecy, the movement of prophets from Phrygia, in a letter to Caricus and Pontius. With it he sent the writings of Claudius Apolinarius, bishop of Hierapolis.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.19, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 30535-30562

lines.text: Serapion writes to the church at Rhossus that on a visit he let the gospel put forward under Peter's name be read, without having read it himself. Having since learned that some there were led into false teaching by it, he will come again soon.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.12, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33692-33715

lines.text: Eusebius writes that when Serapion died, Asclepiades, a confessor in the persecution, became bishop of Antioch, and that Alexander, a bishop then in prison, wrote to the church of Antioch to welcome the news.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.11, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 33558-33606

timeline.when: Paul of Samosata made bishop, about 260
timeline.headline: Paul of Samosata becomes bishop, and his judges say what he taught

lines.when: about the time Dionysius became bishop of Rome
lines.text: Eusebius writes that when Demetrianus died in Antioch, Paul of Samosata received the office of bishop, about the time Dionysius succeeded Xistus at Rome.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.27, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41758-41785

lines.when: about 260, the seventh year of Valerian and Gallienus
lines.text: Eusebius's Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, says that Paul of Samosata was made the fifteenth bishop of Antioch.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 44213-44215; the year is a conversion from the Chronicle's seventh year of Valerian and Gallienus, counting their reign from 253
lines.note: Jerome made the Latin Chronicle more than a century later.

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Paul held low views of Christ, that he was by nature an ordinary man.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.27, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41836-41840

lines.text: The bishops who judged Paul write that he would not confess that the Son of God came down from heaven, and that he said Jesus Christ is from below.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42173-42178

timeline.when: The bishops meet over Paul, date unknown
timeline.headline: Bishops come to Antioch again and again, and Firmilian dies on his third journey

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, was asked to come, but being too old and weak he gave his view by letter.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.27, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41840-41851

lines.text: The bishops write that Dionysius of Alexandria did not think Paul worthy to be written to, and wrote to the whole church at Antioch instead.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42032-42042

lines.text: Eusebius writes that the pastors of the churches hurried to Antioch from every side, as against a man ravaging Christ's flock. Among the most eminent he names Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Gregory and Athenodorus of Pontus, and Helenus of Tarsus, with many presbyters and deacons.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.28, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41859-41892

lines.text: Eusebius writes that the bishops met often and at different times, and that Paul's side tried at every meeting to hide what he taught.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.28, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41894-41899

lines.text: The bishops write that Firmilian came twice and condemned Paul's new teaching. When Paul promised to change his views, Firmilian believed him and put the matter off.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42044-42066

lines.text: The bishops write that Firmilian set out for Antioch again and reached Tarsus, and died there while they were gathered and waiting for him.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42068-42072

timeline.when: Before the last meeting, date unknown
timeline.headline: The bishops charge Paul over his wealth, his throne and the singing in his church
timeline.witness: The bishops' letter, written by the men who judged him, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul, once poor, grew rich on what he took from the brothers, promising for a reward to help people in trouble and then deceiving them.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42084-42101

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul would rather be called ducenarius, an imperial official's title, than bishop, and walked the market places reading and dictating letters, with a bodyguard and crowds before and behind him.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42103-42126

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul built himself a tribunal and a high throne, and a secretum, a private room set apart, like the rulers of the world. He struck his thigh and stamped on the tribunal as he spoke.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42128-42156

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul scolded those who did not cheer and wave handkerchiefs as in the theater, but listened with reverence, as in the house of God.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42156-42160

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul stopped the psalms sung to Jesus Christ as too new, the work of newer men. At Easter, they write, he trained women to sing psalms to himself in the middle of the church.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42165-42168

lines.text: The bishops write that those who sang Paul's praises among the people said he had come down from heaven as an angel, and that he did not stop them.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42178-42201

lines.text: The bishops write that Paul kept two young women with him, women the people of Antioch called subintroductae, those brought into the house, and let his clergy do the same. Even if he did nothing sinful, they write, he should have avoided the suspicion.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42203-42241

lines.text: The bishops write that everyone in Paul's church mourned in private, but feared his tyranny and power too much to accuse him.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42243-42245

timeline.when: The last meeting, in Aurelian's reign by Eusebius's account
timeline.headline: Malchion questions Paul, the bishops cut him off, and Aurelian rules on the church's house

lines.when: in the reign of Aurelian, Eusebius says
lines.text: Eusebius writes that in Aurelian's reign a last meeting of a great many bishops was held. Paul's false teaching was shown before all, and he was cut off from the whole church.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.29, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41936-41954

lines.when: the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Valerian and Gallienus, the Chronicle says
lines.text: Eusebius's Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, sets Paul's fall beside these years: he turned from what all preached and stirred up the heresy of Artemon. Domnus was made bishop of Antioch in his place.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 44278-44287
lines.note: Eusebius's History sets the last meeting under Aurelian instead.

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Malchion, head of the school of Greek learning in Antioch and made a presbyter there for his faith, drew Paul out in a debate that shorthand writers took down. He alone, Eusebius says, could expose a man who hid his mind.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.29, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41977-41984
lines.note: Eusebius says the debate still existed in his day.

lines.text: Jerome writes that Malchion had taught rhetoric at Antioch with great success, that his debate with Paul was still extant, and that he wrote a long letter for the council to Dionysius and Maximus.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 71, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40904-40911
lines.note: Eusebius says the bishops wrote the letter by common consent.

lines.text: Eusebius writes that the bishops, by common consent, wrote a letter to Dionysius, bishop of Rome, and Maximus of Alexandria, and sent it to all the provinces.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41993-42001

lines.text: The bishops write that they have cut Paul off, since he sets himself against God and refuses to obey, and have made Domnus, son of the former bishop Demetrianus, bishop in his place. They ask the churches to write to Domnus and receive from him letters of communion, the letters bishops exchanged to show they shared one church.
lines.reference: The bishops' letter, in Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42274-42314

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Paul refused to give up the church's house, and the emperor Aurelian was petitioned. Aurelian ordered the house given to those to whom the bishops of Italy and Rome wrote, and so Paul was driven out of the church by the worldly power.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42324-42330
lines.note: Eusebius says only that Aurelian decided most equitably, and gives no reason.

lines.text: Athanasius writes that Zenobia was a supporter of Paul of Samosata.
lines.reference: Athanasius, History of the Arians 71, cic/texts/npnf204_athanasius-select-works-letters.xml lines 40311-40315
lines.note: Athanasius wrote in the next century, as an opponent of Paul's teaching.

timeline.when: In the persecution under Maximinus, early in the 4th century
timeline.headline: Lucian, a presbyter of Antioch, dies a martyr at Nicomedia

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Lucian, a presbyter of the church at Antioch whose whole life was excellent, proclaimed Christ before the emperor at Nicomedia, first in a spoken defense and then by his deeds.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VIII.13, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 44730-44735

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Lucian, learned in sacred things, was brought to Nicomedia, where the emperor was staying, gave a defense of his faith before the ruler, and was imprisoned and put to death.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IX.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 48018-48023

lines.text: Jerome writes that Lucian, presbyter of Antioch, studied the Scriptures so closely that in his day some copies of them still bore Lucian's name. He was put to death at Nicomedia and buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 77, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40995-41001

lines.text: John Chrysostom, preaching on Lucian, says that to every question under torture he answered only, I am a Christian: when asked his homeland, his trade and his parents.
lines.reference: John Chrysostom, Homily on the Martyr Lucian, Latin tr. Fronton du Duc, cic/texts/john-chrysostom_homily-martyr-lucian-grc-lat_migne-pg50.txt lines 15435-15440
lines.note: Chrysostom preached late in the 4th century. The sermon is held here only in Latin.

lines.text: Philostorgius writes that Lucian, chained in prison and kept from the church and the altar, lay on his back and offered the sacrament on his own breast. He gave it to the Christians around him.
lines.reference: Philostorgius, Church History, in Photius's summary, tr. Walford, cic/texts/philostorgius_ecclesiastical-history_walford1855.txt line 136
lines.note: Philostorgius's account, known only through a later summary.

lines.text: Eusebius's Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, says that Constantine rebuilt Drepana in Bithynia in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, and named it Helenopolis after his mother.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 45078-45080

timeline.headline: Arius names himself a pupil of Lucian, and later writers look back on the council against Paul

lines.text: Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, writes to Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, that his bishop drove him out of the city for not agreeing that the Son always was, as God always was. Arius says the Son has a beginning, and God has none.
lines.reference: Arius, Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret, Church History I.4, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 6025-6031,  6045-6046; Arius a presbyter of Alexandria, Theodoret I.1, lines 5278-5283

lines.text: Arius closes his letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia by calling him fellow-Lucianist.
lines.reference: Arius, Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret, Church History I.4, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 6063-6064

lines.text: Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, writes that Arius's teaching rivals that of Paul of Samosata, cut off by a council of all the bishops. Lucian, he writes, came after Paul and kept out of communion with the bishops for many years, and Arius and his party are shoots of the same stock.
lines.reference: Alexander of Alexandria, Letter, in Theodoret, Church History I.3, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 5752-5775

lines.text: Philostorgius names pupils of Lucian who became bishops: Eusebius of Nicomedia, Maris of Chalcedon, Theognis of Nicaea and Leontius, later of Antioch. He says some of them sacrificed to the gods under the tyrants, and that Lucian helped bring them back to repentance.
lines.reference: Philostorgius, Church History, in Photius's summary, tr. Walford, cic/texts/philostorgius_ecclesiastical-history_walford1855.txt line 138

lines.text: The council of Nicaea rules that the Paulianists, Paul's followers, who come over to the Catholic Church must be baptized again, and that their clergy found blameless are to be baptized and ordained again.
lines.reference: Council of Nicaea, canon 19, tr. Percival, cic/texts/npnf214_seven-ecumenical-councils.xml lines 5296-5302

lines.text: Sozomen writes that bishops meeting at Antioch said they had found a creed written entirely by Lucian. He does not know whether that was true, or said to give their document a martyr's weight.
lines.reference: Sozomen, Church History III.5, cic/texts/npnf202_socrates-sozomen-ecclesiastical-histories.xml lines 31024-31035

lines.text: Athanasius answers bishops who said the council that deposed Paul had written that the Son is not coessential, of one being, with the Father. He says he does not have their letter, and that those bishops took the word in a bodily sense.
lines.reference: Athanasius, On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia, cic/texts/npnf204_athanasius-select-works-letters.xml lines 58970-58981,  59053-59057
lines.note: Athanasius speaks of the seventy who deposed Paul, line 58995.

lines.text: Hilary of Poitiers writes that the fathers who condemned Paul rejected the word homoousion, because Paul had used it to teach that God was single and undivided. He says eighty bishops once rejected it.
lines.reference: Hilary, On the Councils 81, 86, tr. Watson, cic/texts/npnf209_hilary-poitiers-john-damascus.xml lines 9607-9611,  9772-9773

lines.text: Basil writes that the synods on Paul of Samosata found fault with the word homoousion, holding that it set forth both an essence and what is derived from it.
lines.reference: Basil, Letter 52, tr. Jackson, cic/texts/npnf208_basil-letters-select-works.xml lines 27366-27368,  27402-27407

uncertain: When the last meeting was held. Eusebius puts the final synod in the reign of Aurelian. Jerome's Chronicle sets Paul's fall, and Domnus made bishop in his place, beside the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Gallienus. No old source gives the year as a number.
How many bishops condemned him. Eusebius says a great many. Athanasius speaks of the seventy who deposed him, and Hilary of eighty bishops.
Who wrote the bishops' letter. Eusebius says the bishops prepared it by common consent. Jerome says Malchion wrote it on the council's behalf, to Dionysius of Rome and Maximus of Alexandria.
Malchion's questioning. Eusebius judges that Malchion alone was able to detect Paul, who hid his mind and deceived the others.

Why the council refused the word homoousios, the word Nicaea later used to say the Son is of one being with the Father. In the 350s, bishops wary of Nicaea's word said the council against Paul had refused it. Athanasius, who says he did not have their letter, answers that those bishops took the word in a bodily sense, because Paul had argued that it would make three essences. Hilary says Paul had used it to teach that God was single and undivided. Basil says the bishops held that it set forth both an essence and what is derived from it. None of the three quotes the letter, and they disagree on the reason.

The bishops' other charges, all from the letter of the men who judged him. Once poor, they wrote, he grew rich on what he extorted from the brethren, promising for a reward to help people in trouble and then deceiving them. He would rather be called ducenarius, an imperial official's title, than bishop. His singers called him an angel come down from heaven, and he did not stop them. He kept two young women with him and let his clergy keep women too, though the bishops grant he may have done nothing sinful and say he should have avoided the suspicion. In his church, they wrote, all mourned in private, but so feared his tyranny and power that they dared not accuse him.

The bishop of Alexandria, Dionysius, was asked to come but was too old and weak. Eusebius and the bishops' letter say he gave his view by letter, and would not address Paul, but wrote to the whole church at Antioch.
In Paul's place the bishops appointed Domnus, son of Demetrianus, the bishop before Paul, and asked the churches to write to him and receive letters of communion from him.
Why the emperor ruled as he did. Eusebius gives no reason, only that Aurelian decided the matter "most equitably".
Lucian and the Scriptures. Jerome says Lucian was so diligent in the study of the Scriptures that in his day certain copies of the Scriptures still bore Lucian's name.

Lucian's pupils. Philostorgius, a historian friendly to Arius's side, known only through a hostile summary of his book, names pupils who became bishops of Nicomedia, Chalcedon, Nicaea and Antioch, and one at Tarsus. He says some of them sacrificed to the gods under the persecutors, and that Lucian helped bring them back to repentance.

Lucian's creed. Later bishops meeting at Antioch said they had found a creed written entirely by Lucian. Sozomen did not know whether this was true, or whether they said it to give their document a martyr's weight.

quotationOriginals.modern: He stopped the psalms to our Lord Jesus Christ, as if they were too new, the work of newer men. But on the great day of Easter he trains women to sing psalms to himself, in the middle of the church. Anyone who heard them would shudder.
quotationOriginals.printed: stops the psalms to our Lord Jesus Christ, as being the modern productions of modern men, and trains women to sing psalms to himself in the midst of the church on the great day of the passover, which any one might shudder to hear
quotationOriginals.work: The bishops' letter against Paul of Samosata, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 7, chapter 30, tr. McGiffert
quotationOriginals.original: ψαλμοὺς δὲ τοὺς uir εἰς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν παύσας ὡς δὴ veo-τέρους καὶ νεωτέρων ἀνδρῶν συγγράμματα. εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐν μέσῃ 77 ἐχχλησίᾳ τῇ μεγάλῃ τοῦ πάσχα ἡμέρᾳ ψαλμῳδεῖν γυναῖκας παρασχευάζων. ὧν xai ἀχούσας ἄν τις φρίξειεν
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The rendering is made from Schwartz's Greek, printed here as the scan reads it. The scan has faults: uir for μὲν, veo for νεω, 77 for τῇ before ἐκκλησίᾳ, xai for καὶ, and chi for kappa in several words; its margin line number and quotation marks are left out. Rufinus's Latin in the same volume (in medio ecclesiae, lines 11951-11955) and McGiffert's English confirm the reading.

quotationOriginals.modern: To each question he answered only, I am a Christian. When the torturer asked, What is your homeland? I am a Christian, he said. What is your trade? I am a Christian. Who are your parents? To all of it he said, I am a Christian.
quotationOriginals.printed: ille vero ad unamquamque interrogationem tantum respondebat, Christianus sum, ac dicente tortore, Quanam ex patria ortus es? Christianus sum, ait; Quam artem profiteris ? Christianus sum; Quibus parentibus natus es? ille. vero ad omnia dicebat, Christianus sum
quotationOriginals.work: John Chrysostom, Homily on the Martyr Lucian, Latin tr. Fronton du Duc (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 50)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The rendering is made from Fronton du Duc's Latin translation of Chrysostom's Greek. The Greek is not legible in the held scan, and no English is held. The scan prints a stray full stop after the second ille.

quotationOriginals.modern: I pray you fare well in the Lord, remembering our troubles, fellow-Lucianist.
quotationOriginals.printed: I bid thee farewell in the Lord, remembering our afflictions, my fellow-Lucianist
quotationOriginals.work: Arius, Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, in Theodoret, Church History, Book 1, chapter 4, tr. Jackson
quotationOriginals.original: Ἐρρῶσϑαί σε iv κυρίῳ εὔχομαι, μεμνημένον τῶν ϑλίψεων ἡμῶν, 5 Συλλουκιανιστὰ
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The rendering is made from the Greek of the letter as Epiphanius copies it, printed here as Oehler's scan reads it: iv for ἐν, and 5 a note mark; a stray line of scan marks between the two lines is left out. Jackson's English, from Theodoret's copy, confirms the reading.
